analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill had zero cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the federal estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, the taxes paid when very large amounts of wealth pass to heirs or others. The repeal would apply to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2001. Only a small share of the largest estates ever owed the estate tax, and a 2001 law had already scheduled a temporary repeal for 2010.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — roughly the wealthiest one or two percent of families, those whose estates exceeded the exemption amount — would save the entire tax bill on inherited wealth. Very wealthy families making large lifetime gifts would also gain. Estate planning focused on avoiding these taxes would become unnecessary for affected families.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S2][S3].
Applies retroactively in effect to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2001, so estates of people who died after that date would owe no tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which loses the revenue these taxes raise from large estates, leaving other taxpayers to make up the difference through borrowing or cuts to federal programs. Charities could also lose, since the estate tax currently gives wealthy families an incentive to leave money to charity to reduce the tax.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax paid almost exclusively by the largest estates, so its cost falls on the general Treasury while its benefit is concentrated among the wealthiest families [S2][S3].

Repealing the gift tax alongside the estate tax removes the backstop that prevents people from escaping the income tax transfer system through lifetime gifts, a broader loss of revenue than estate tax repeal alone [S3].
The estate tax is one of the few taxes that encourages large charitable bequests; permanent repeal would remove that incentive and could reduce charitable giving [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to heirs of very large estates, while the cost — lost federal revenue in the tens of billions per year — is spread across everyone who relies on or funds federal programs. The gift tax repeal widens the revenue loss beyond estate taxation itself. On balance the bill is a large, permanent transfer to the wealthiest families paid for out of general revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Max Sandlin, a Texas Democrat, introduced the bill on April 15, 2002 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee never scheduled the bill, no vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal revenue and the programs it funds were protected, and the estate tax's incentive for charitable bequests remained intact. Families with large estates continued to owe the tax, though a 2001 law already scheduled its temporary repeal in 2010.

for.name: Rep. Max Sandlin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral, never scheduling it for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a single Democrat with no cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc ever took a position on it.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently eliminated the estate tax, a levy paid almost entirely by the largest estates, while the lost revenue would otherwise support federal programs funded by taxpayers generally.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: Repeal would end a large body of tax-driven estate planning work, costing advisors fees, while their clients would save far more in taxes.
The estate tax gives wealthy families a reason to leave large charitable bequests; permanent repeal would remove that incentive and could shrink donations.
